newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine shares tumble, peso hits new low.
newsitem.headline: Philippine shares tumble, peso hits new low.

text.p: Philippine financial markets plunged in early Monday trading, shaken by the sharp drop in U.S. shares late last week and the continued turmoil in southeast Asian currencies.
The bearish mood dragged the Philippine peso to a record low and battered the country's stock market.
Traders blamed much of the rout in the stock market on last Friday's slump in New York where the Dow Jones index scored its second-biggest point loss ever and steepest fall since October 1987.
"The market is so bearish that any bad news such as the Dow's fall is magnified. Add to that the continued turmoil in the currency," said Noel Reyes, vice-president at Anscor-Hagedorn Securities.

But it was the peso's fall to a new low in the morning which gave shares another push lower and by late morning the main index had fallen 4.12 percent to 2,348.10 points, well below the latest support levels.
"Definitely it's the peso hitting 30 to a dollar that's making the market move this way," said Cilette Liboro, research head at Orion-Squire Capital.
Traders said buyers had pulled out of the market, waiting to see when prices hit bottom before coming back in.
One of the most active issues was Philippine Long Distance Telephone Co, the country's biggest telecommunications firm, which fell 2.85 percent to 850 pesos.
Foreign selling also hit Manila Electric Co.
Its B shares, which are open to foreign investors, dropped 7.56 percent to 110 pesos.

As widely predicted, the peso fell to a new low, dipping below the previous record low of 30 to the dollar it hit last month when the government was forced by repeated speculative attacks to allow a de facto devaluation of the currency.
Though the peso has since fallen less than many other currencies in the region, fresh turmoil in the market generally has put renewed pressure on the Philippine currency.
However, the central bank, which in recent weeks has imposed a series of restrictions to limit any more damage from speculators, kept out of the currency market in the morning, traders said.

"There's a common strategy among the central banks in the region to let their currencies seek their own levels - which should bring us closer to stability earlier," an analyst at one foreign brokerage house said.
"There's a natural strong demand for dollars because of the import season. Why fight against it? The best strategy is to let it float, to make it expensive for importers," he added.
